title: How to Help Someone With an Eating Disorder: What Works
summary: How to help someone with an eating disorder, step by step: noticing signs, starting the conversation, supporting treatment, and caring for yourself.
body_markdown:
Figuring out how to help someone with an eating disorder can feel overwhelming. It's natural to want to help … and to worry about getting it wrong.


“Sometimes we worry about overstepping or saying something we're not supposed to say,” says[Jen Simmons, PhDc, LPC](https://equip.health/articles/author/jen-simmons) , Equip Lead Therapist. “But if someone is struggling with anything, sometimes they're afraid to ask for help. Support makes a world of difference.”


The good news is that you don't need all the answers or the perfect words to make a positive change. Loved ones can play an important role in recognizing concerns, encouraging treatment, and supporting recovery.


And you shouldn’t wait for a crisis before you speak up. Here's how to show up for someone you love, even when you're not sure what they need.


*If your loved one is in immediate danger or experiencing a medical emergency, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. For suicidal thoughts or emotional distress, call or text 988 for free, confidential crisis support.*


## **How can you help someone with an eating disorder?**


You can help someone with an eating disorder by learning about their condition, talking about your concerns, encouraging treatment, and offering ongoing support. You don't need to be an expert—what matters most is approaching them with compassion and a willingness to listen.


While everyone's needs are different and your role may change over time,[Hannah Bishop, LPC](https://equip.health/articles/author/hannah-bishop) , lead therapist at Equip, says there are some key ways to make a difference:


- **Notice and learn:** Pay attention to changes in your loved one's eating habits, mood, or behavior, and educate yourself about eating disorders.
- **Talk about it:** Share your concerns gently and without judgment, focusing on what you've noticed rather than making assumptions. Give your loved one space to share their feelings, even if they're not ready to acknowledge a problem.
- **Support treatment and recovery:** Encourage your loved one to seek professional help, offer practical assistance when it's welcome, and support them throughout recovery.
- **Take care of yourself:** Set boundaries and seek support when you need it. Helping someone through an eating disorder can be emotionally demanding, and your well-being matters, too.


## **Noticing signs and educating yourself**


It isn't always easy to tell if someone is struggling with an eating disorder.[Early signs](https://equip.health/articles/understanding-eds/early-signs-of-an-eating-disorder) and symptoms vary, and some behaviors can easily be mistaken for healthy habits (especially in our[diet culture](https://equip.health/articles/diet-culture-and-society/what-is-diet-culture) , which often praises weight loss).


Some common[warning signs of an eating disorder](https://equip.health/articles/understanding-eds/subtle-signs-of-an-eating-disorder) include skipping meals, cutting out entire food groups, becoming anxious about eating with others, following rigid exercise routines, or withdrawing from friends and family. You might also notice[changes](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12882398/) in a loved one’s mood, energy, or relationship with their body.


It's important to remember that you can't tell whether someone has an eating disorder just by looking at them. Even if their[weight hasn't changed](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK567717/) or they seem healthy on the outside, they may still be struggling.


That's why learning more about eating disorders can be so valuable. The better you understand what your loved one might be going through, the better equipped you'll be to support them. These trusted resources are a good place to start:


- [Equip](https://equip.health/articles) : Equip is an eating disorder treatment provider that also offers accessible information about eating disorders, treatment, and recovery.
- [Families Empowered and Supporting Treatment for Eating Disorders (FEAST)](https://feast-ed.org/) : Education, practical tools, and support for caregivers of people with eating disorders.
- [Academy for Eating Disorders](https://www.aedweb.org/) : Research-based network that advances eating disorder prevention, education, and treatment.


## **How to bring up your concerns**


You don't need to be certain someone has an eating disorder to speak up. Changes in eating habits, exercise, mood, or body image are all reasons to check in, even without visible physical changes. Trust your gut, and don't wait for a crisis. Instead, find a calm, private moment to share what you've noticed with compassion and without judgment.


And while there's no perfect script for these conversations, how you approach them matters. “Keep in mind that you may be speaking with someone experiencing emotional dysregulation and a malnourished brain, which can trigger defensive reactions,” says Bishop. “Throughout the interaction, maintain a calm, gentle, and warm demeanor.”


Bishop recommends a few other ways to help your loved one feel more comfortable opening up, including:


- **Choose the right moment:** Find a private setting to share your concerns, rather than bringing them up during meals or heated moments.
- **Be specific about what you've noticed:** Some people with eating disorders struggle to recognize they're ill (a symptom known as[anosognosia](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12447322/) ), while others believe their behaviors are beneficial. Because of this, it’s important to focus on observable changes rather than accusations. “For many people, it's not denial. It's that their brain doesn't recognize it,” says J.D. Ouellette, Equip’s director of Lived Experience. “It's harder to say objective things aren't happening.”
- **Use “I” statements:** “Utilizing ‘I’ statements rather than accusatory ‘you’ statements can minimize defensive responses,” says Bishop.
- **Validate their feelings while expressing concern:** Ouellette recommends using the power of “and” to acknowledge your loved one's feelings without backing away from your concerns. For example: “I know this conversation is difficult, and I'm bringing it up because I love you and I'm worried.”
- **Avoid focusing on appearance or food choices:** Comments about body size or what someone eats can increase shame or defensiveness. Focus on their well-being instead.
- **Keep the door open:** Your loved one may not be ready to talk or accept help right away. Let them know you're available whenever they want to talk.

## **What to do if they deny it or don’t want help**


If your loved one denies having an eating disorder or refuses treatment, stay patient and continue offering support without pressure. They may not recognize that they're struggling or have[mixed feelings about recovery](https://equip.health/articles/treatment-and-recovery/ambivalence-eating-disorder-recovery) . Whatever the reason, resistance doesn't mean your support isn't helping.


Bishop and Ouellet encourage loved ones to maintain a caring connection, even when met with anger or defensiveness. They recommend that you:


- **Continue to invite them:** “Let them know they are welcomed, valued, and loved,” Ouellette says. “Inviting them lets them know that you're there for them, even if the eating disorder may make them say no to you.”
- **Remind them they matter:** Show them that they're valued for who they are, not what they eat or how they look. ”Reassure them that seeking help is a sign of strength and that they deserve care, support, and a full life,” says Bishop.
- **Make getting help easier:** Offer to research treatment providers,[check Equip’s insurance coverage](https://equip.health/insurance-screener) , or accompany them to an appointment.


As difficult as it can be, you generally can't make another adult seek treatment if they're not ready. The exception is when their safety is at immediate risk, though laws around[involuntary treatment](https://www.samhsa.gov/resource/ebp/civil-commitment-mental-health-care-continuum-historical-trends-principles-law) vary by state.


If you're feeling stuck or unsure what to try next, our guide to[Helping Someone Who Doesn't Want Eating Disorder Treatment](https://equip.health/articles/treatment-and-recovery/what-to-do-if-your-child-resists-eating-disorder-treatment) offers more ways to navigate these challenges.


## **How to support someone during treatment and recovery**


You can support someone through eating disorder treatment and recovery by listening to their needs, offering practical help, and being patient through challenges. Remember that your job isn't to fix the eating disorder, but to remind your loved one that they don't have to face it alone.


What that looks like depends on your relationship and your loved one’s needs during recovery. Whether they're receiving outpatient treatment or a higher[level of care](https://equip.health/articles/treatment-and-recovery/eating-disorder-treatment-options) , here are some meaningful ways to show up.


### **Ways to take action**


One of the simplest ways to help is to ask your loved one what they need rather than assuming you know. Some people appreciate company during meals, while others simply want someone to listen.


You can also try offering something specific. This could include things like:


- Inviting them out to an ice cream date, and they can bring their own food
- Inviting them to dinner, and have them pick out their meal ahead of time
- Attending a therapy session with them
- Researching providers
- [Booking their consultation call](https://my.equip.health/) with Equip
- Spending quality time with the person in a way that doesn't revolve around food or body (watching movies together, pottery, reading, games). This offers a nice break for the person going through the ED and maintains a positive relationship.


It's also important to recognize the limits of your role. “You're not a trained therapist, so you probably don't know what to do. And that's okay,” says Simmons. “You're not here to fix it; you're here to support your loved one.”


If your loved one is in treatment, let their team guide their care while you focus on offering encouragement. You can always ask if your loved one (with their team’s approval) would like you to be involved in their care plan.[Involving loved ones in adult treatment](https://equip.health/articles/treatment-and-recovery/adult-eating-disorders-family-involvement-in-treatment) provides crucial support and makes recovery feel less isolating, according to the[European Eating Disorders Review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8246805/) .


And if your loved one becomes angry or defensive, try not to take it personally. Eating disorders can affect how people think, feel, and respond to others, especially when malnutrition is involved, per the journal[Focus](https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.focus.20230042) .


“Developing the clarity and self-awareness needed to accept help can take a significant amount of time,” says Bishop. “Keep reaching out, checking in, and offering a safe, supportive presence.”


### **Your own beliefs about food and bodies**


“This is critical. We all live in diet culture. It's the sea we swim in,” Ouellette says. Indeed, everyday habits like praising weight loss or criticizing our own bodies can reinforce harmful beliefs without us realizing it.


Simmons suggests noticing when conversations about food or body size make you uncomfortable and getting curious about why. Challenging these assumptions takes practice, but it can help you create a more supportive environment.


Learning about diet culture and weight-inclusive approaches like[Health at Every Size (HAES)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11493725/) is also a good place to start, as is becoming more mindful of everyday comments and behaviors so you can[avoid triggering](https://equip.health/articles/understanding-eds/how-to-avoid-triggering-someone-with-an-eating-disorder) someone with an eating disorder.


### **When setbacks happen**


[Recovery isn't linear](https://equip.health/articles/treatment-and-recovery/nonlinear-eating-disorder-recovery) . Eating disorder relapses and[setbacks are common](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S002239562300002X?via%3Dihub) , but they don't erase the progress someone has made.


“It's not that your loved one 'didn't want it enough' or that they like living like this,” Ouellette says. “It's just the nature of the illness. It's very hard to treat.”


If you notice[signs of relapse](https://equip.health/articles/treatment-and-recovery/signs-of-eating-disorder-relapse) , gently share your concerns and encourage your loved one to reconnect with their treatment team. Above all, try to approach setbacks with compassion rather than blame. Recovery can be difficult even when someone genuinely wants to get better, and your continued support can make a difference.

## **How to help based on your relationship**


The best way to support someone with an eating disorder depends partly on your relationship. Compassion, patience, and open communication are always important, but your connection to each other can shape what kind of help is appropriate.


### **If it’s your partner or spouse**


Having a partner with an eating disorder can affect many parts of your life together—after all, you share a home, meals, and finances. You may[be able to help](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/10640266.2023.2206753?url_ver=Z39.88-2003&rfr_id=ori:rid:crossref.org&rfr_dat=cr_pub%20%200pubmed) by offering support around meals, taking on household responsibilities, or helping coordinate appointments.


But remember that you're their partner, not their treatment provider. It's important to[nurture your relationship outside of treatment](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5519332/) so you’re able to connect as a couple rather than letting the eating disorder become the focus of every interaction.


### **If it’s a friend or roommate**


One of the most meaningful things you can do to support a friend with an eating disorder is offer consistent support. Check in regularly and keep inviting them to spend time together, even if they decline, says Bishop. Just remember that you don't have to take on the responsibility of helping them recover on your own, adds Simmons.


### **If it’s your adult child**


It's natural to want to step in and help your adult child with an eating disorder. But they may want to make their own decisions about treatment, and that's important to respect. You can still[play a meaningful role in their recovery](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9245299/) by asking what they need and offering help in ways they're comfortable with.


### **If it’s your sibling**


[Having a sibling with an eating disorder](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7338552/) can bring up complicated emotions. Try to keep your connection strong by checking in, spending time together, and reminding them that your relationship is about more than their eating disorder.


It's also important to recognize your own needs. You may feel responsible for protecting your sibling or keeping the peace at home, but you don't have to manage their recovery. You can be a caring, supportive presence while still setting boundaries and making space for your well-being.


### **If it’s a coworker or someone you manage**


If you're worried about a coworker, find a private moment to check in. Focus on changes you've noticed in their well-being or work rather than their appearance, and avoid making assumptions about what they're going through.


You can point them toward[workplace resources](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12350497/) , talk through what accommodations might help, or encourage them to seek professional support. Above all, respect their privacy and let them decide what they're comfortable sharing.


## **If the person you’re worried about is your child**


Watching your kid struggle can be frightening, especially when you're not sure[how to help a child with an eating disorder](https://equip.health/articles/understanding-eds/how-to-help-a-child-with-an-eating-disorder) . But as a parent or caregiver, you can play a powerful role in their recovery, and you don't have to navigate it alone.


Unlike adults, children and teens often need more hands-on support from their parents during treatment. In fact,[family-based treatment (FBT)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6764593/) , which is the most-recommended approach for treating eating disorders in young people, directly involves parents in the recovery process.


And if your child is[resisting treatment](https://equip.health/articles/treatment-and-recovery/what-to-do-if-your-child-resists-eating-disorder-treatment) , know that this isn't unusual. Eating disorders can make it difficult for them to recognize the seriousness of their illness, says Bishop, and fear of the changes that come with recovery can make accepting help especially challenging. That said, your child's resistance should never prevent seeking treatment; resistance is common, and treatment will help them. Resistance doesn't necessarily mean your child doesn't want help, and it's something their treatment team can help you navigate.


## **How to take care of yourself while you help**


Supporting someone through an eating disorder can take a real emotional and physical toll, according to[Equip’s research on caregivers](https://equip.health/articles/news-and-research/caregiver-burden-eating-disorders) . That's why it's so important to recognize and care for your own needs, too. You can be there for someone you love without putting your own well-being on hold.


Here are a few ways to take care of yourself:


- **Set boundaries:** Boundaries are a way to communicate what you need while continuing to offer support, says Ouellette. Be honest about how much time and energy you can give, step away from hurtful conversations, and make space for your own life.
- **Talk to a therapist:** Having someone to help you process your emotions and navigate difficult situations can make the experience less overwhelming.
- **Connect with others who understand:**[Support groups](https://equip.health/articles/treatment-and-recovery/eating-disorder-support-groups) can help you feel less alone and more supported.
- **Explore support through Equip:** Equip’s[resources for loved ones](https://equip.health/articles/tags/for%20loved%20ones) can help you navigate the recovery process.

## **When to get emergency help**


If someone with an eating disorder shows signs of a medical emergency or is at immediate risk of harming themselves, seek emergency care right away. Eating disorders can cause life-threatening complications, and you shouldn't wait for your loved one to agree to treatment if their safety is at risk.


Warning signs that need immediate attention include:


- Fainting, loss of consciousness, or seizures
- Chest pain, an irregular heartbeat, or difficulty breathing
- Severe weakness, confusion, or disorientation
- Severe dehydration, including very little urine or an inability to keep fluids down
- Suicidal thoughts, self-harm, or threats of self-harm


Medical complications can happen at any weight or body size, even if your loved one seems "[not sick enough](https://equip.health/articles/understanding-eds/not-sick-enough-eating-disorder-treatment) ." If they're in immediate danger, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department. For suicidal thoughts or emotional distress, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in the U.S.


It also helps to prepare before an emergency happens. “If you suspect someone might have an emergency, do your homework in advance,” says Ouellette. “Our system comes with many limitations and a lot of lack of understanding.” Researching hospitals with experience treating eating disorders can help you know where to turn if your loved one[needs hospitalization](https://equip.health/articles/understanding-eds/inpatient-hospitalization-eating-disorder) .


## **The bottom line**


You don’t need to have all the answers to help someone with an eating disorder. What’s most important is showing up with compassion, listening without judgment, and offering support.


Recovery is possible, even when progress feels slow. And while you can't recover for someone else, your continued support can make a meaningful difference. “There is a path forward. It won't be easy, and a lot of things in life aren't easy. We can do hard things,” Ouellette says.


## **FAQ**


### **Do eating disorders ever go away on their own?**


No, eating disorders do not go away on their own. They are serious,[brain-based mental illnesses](https://equip.health/articles/understanding-eds/braindisorders) that require professional support. At minimum, this includes a therapist, dietitian, and a medical professional.


### **Should I praise my loved one when they eat?**


It's generally best to avoid commenting on how much or what your loved one eats unless their treatment team recommends otherwise. Even well-intentioned praise can create pressure or draw unwanted attention to eating. Instead, offer encouragement that focuses on their efforts and well-being.


### **Is helping a man with an eating disorder different?**


The same principles of compassion, patience, and professional support apply to everyone. However, because[eating disorders in boys and men](https://equip.health/articles/understanding-eds/eating-disorders-in-men-and-boys) are often overlooked or misunderstood, they may face additional stigma or have a harder time recognizing their symptoms and seeking help.
